newsitem.title: USA: Keep hedges trimmed, get a barking dog.
newsitem.headline: Keep hedges trimmed, get a barking dog.

text.p: (Part 2 of a two-part series on personal and home security. Last week's column dealt with personal protection agents.)
By Judith Schoolman
More than 1.5 million home burglaries occur each year, but 90 percent of these crimes could have been prevented, experts say.
Basically, there are three easy steps to keeping a house safe, and they don't cost very much. Keep surrounding hedges trimmed, get photosensitive flood lights and get a noisy dog.
"Light, time and noise are a homeowner's greatest weapons in the fight to prevent a home burglary," according to the Insurance Information Institute (III), a trade group.
"A burglar will think twice about breaking into your home if he/she has to manoeuvre in a well-lit yard and if you make it both time-consuming and noisy to get into your house," III says.

When making sure your house or apartment is burglar-proof, first think like a burglar. Determine how easy it is to tell if no one is home, how easily windows and doors can be pried open or how easily valuables can be viewed from outside.
Keep hedges trimmed, taking away a would-be burglar's hiding place. Sacrificing a little privacy for a lot of security may be a worthwhile tradeoff.
Keep lights on and the television going while you are away to give the appearance that someone is in the house.

No need to get an attack dog. In fact, a specially trained security or attack dog is inappropriate for the average household and requires a highly trained handler. Any dog with a loud bark adds a tremendous amount of security to a home.
Many would-be criminals want an easy in and an easy out. If it takes more than five minutes to get into a house or apartment, they'll likely take off.

Strong doors, either solid hardwood or metal at least 1-3/4 inches thick, should have strong locks. If you hire a locksmith, choose one with care. Always select a well-established locksmith business that is bonded and insured. If in doubt, check with your local Better Business Bureau.
A good time to change locks in your home or apartment is when an unhappy domestic worker leaves your employ.
Burglar alarm systems are a more expensive and sometimes complicated addition to a home security programme but might be appropriate in some circumstances.

If you decide to install a burgler alarm system, experts advise contacting your local police or fire department, which might have alarm system specialists. Casualty insurance carriers also usually have a specialist who can recommend equipment and steer you from unscrupulous installation firms.
Advice from alarm installers and manufacturers may not be totally objective.
Avoid buying a system by mail or from any company other than one that specialises in the sale, service and installation of such systems.
"As a rule, the longer the warranty, the better the system," according to "How to Protect Yourself from Crime," published by Reader's Digest.

According to author Ira A. Lipman, president of security service company Guardsmark Inc., if you decide to install a burglar alarm system, it is important to have a source of emergency power for the system if normal power supplies are cut, "such as a fire or deliberate interruption of power."
According to Consumer Reports, a burglar alarm can reduce the likelihood that your house will be robbed by as much as 80 percent, but only if you choose a reliable system and use it correctly.
Lipman writes in "How to Protect Yourself from Crime" that the less people know about the steps you take to secure your property, the more secure you will be.

Many houses display alarm decals when, in reality, they are not protected by an alarm. "Unfortunately, the professional burglar generally knows this...the amateur burgler, on the other hand, is generally more easily deterred by exterior warnings," he writes.
When improving the security of your home, make sure you don't turn it into such a fortress that you can not make a speedy exit in the event of a fire or other emergency.
Keeping unwanted people out of the house is one thing. Home security also includes making sure the people who come inside are trustworthy.

When hiring a person work in your home as a baby sitter or maid, always check references completely. If a prospective employee cannot provide references, it is advised that you contact a reputable investigative agency, or request a records check from the police department of the area where the prospective employee has lived.
"The truth of the matter is that an alarming number of applicants for domestic positions are actually subjects of outstanding arrest warrants," Lipman writes.
Check the immediate members of the applicant's family as well. "A maid whose spouse has had a number of convictions for breaking and entering is hardly an ideal employment prospect," he says.

For more information on home security, send for the free brochure, "Home Security Basics." Send a stamped, self-addressed envelope to Insurance Information Institute, Attn: FB, 110 William Street, New York, N.Y. 10038.
